questions.problem:
$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ to the basis $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ is given above. Find $[x]_{C}$ given that $x=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4{b}_{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $x=2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+4{b}_{3},$ we have 

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 12 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-5)}[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=3{c}_{1}-3{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 2-1\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 5 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 13 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}13 & 7 \\ -11 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$

Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 1 \\ -6 & 19 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 22 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}22 & 19 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}22 & 19 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
